title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given a list of integers nums and a window size k, slide a window of size k from the left end to the right end of the list, one position at a time. Return a list containing the maximum value of each window position. Aim for O(n).
hints: Checking the max of every window separately is O(n * k), too slow for large inputs.
Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. The front is always the current window maximum.
Before adding a new index, pop smaller values from the back. Pop the front if it has left the window.

title: Moving Average Stream
description: Numbers arrive one at a time from a stream. After each number arrives, report the average of the last size numbers received (or of all numbers so far, if fewer than size have arrived). Return the list of reported averages, each rounded down to an integer (integer division). All values are non-negative.
hints: Keep the numbers currently in the window in a queue.
Keep a running total. Add each new number, and subtract the oldest one when the queue grows larger than size.
reference_solution:
def solve(size, values):
    window = []
    total = 0
    out = []
    for v in values:
        window.append(v)
        total += v
        if len(window) > size:
            total -= window.pop(0)
        out.append(total // len(window))
    return out

title: Range Sum Queries
description: Given a list of integers nums and a list of queries, where each query is [left, right] (0-indexed, both ends included), return a list with the sum of nums[left..right] for each query. Aim for O(1) per query after an O(n) preparation step.

examples.explanation: 1+2+3 = 6, 2+3+4 = 9, and the last query is just 5.

hints: Summing each range separately is too slow when there are many queries.
Build a prefix array where prefix[i] is the sum of the first i elements. A range sum is then a difference of two prefix values.

title: Meeting Rooms Needed
description: Each meeting is an interval [start, end). Return the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two meetings in the same room overlap. A meeting that ends at time t does not overlap a meeting that starts at time t. An empty list needs 0 rooms.

examples.explanation: The first meeting overlaps both others, but those two do not overlap each other.

hints: Sort all start times and all end times separately.
Walk through the start times. Before counting a new meeting, free a room for every meeting that has already ended by that start time. Track the largest number of rooms in use.
reference_solution:
def solve(intervals):
    starts = sorted(i[0] for i in intervals)
    ends = sorted(i[1] for i in intervals)
    cur = 0
    best = 0
    e = 0
    for s in starts:
        while e < len(ends) and ends[e] <= s:
            e += 1
            cur -= 1
        cur += 1
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

title: Non-Overlapping Intervals
description: Given a list of intervals [start, end], return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at an endpoint (such as [1, 2] and [2, 3]) do not overlap.

examples.explanation: Removing [1, 3] leaves three intervals that do not overlap.

hints: Think of it as keeping as many intervals as possible.
Sort by end time. Keep an interval if it starts at or after the end of the last kept interval, otherwise remove it.

title: Kth Smallest in Sorted Matrix
description: You are given a square matrix in which every row is sorted in ascending order and every column is sorted in ascending order. Return the k-th smallest value in the whole matrix (k is 1-indexed, and repeated values count separately).
hints: Flattening and sorting works, but it ignores the sorted structure.
Put the first value of each row in a min-heap along with its row and column. Pop the smallest k times, each time pushing the next value from the same row.

title: Shortest Path in Grid
description: A grid contains 0 (open cell) and 1 (blocked cell). Starting at the top-left cell, you may move up, down, left or right into open cells. Return the minimum number of moves needed to reach the bottom-right cell, or -1 if it cannot be reached. If the start or the end cell is blocked, or the grid is empty, return -1. A grid with one open cell needs 0 moves.

examples.explanation: Go right twice, then down twice.

hints: Every move costs the same, so breadth-first search finds the shortest path.
Keep a queue of (row, column, distance) and a set of visited cells. Stop when you pop the bottom-right cell.

title: Number of Connected Components
description: An undirected graph has n nodes numbered 0 to n - 1 and a list of edges [a, b]. Return the number of connected components. A node with no edges is its own component. Edges may repeat or connect a node to itself.

examples.explanation: Nodes 0, 1, 2 form one component and nodes 3, 4 form another.

hints: Start by assuming every node is its own component, so the count is n.
Use union-find. Each time an edge joins two nodes that are in different sets, merge them and reduce the count by 1.

title: Word Ladder Length
description: Given a begin word, an end word and a list of allowed words (all the same length, lowercase), find the length of the shortest sequence that starts at the begin word and ends at the end word, where each step changes exactly one letter and every word after the first must be in the allowed list. Count the words in the sequence, including the begin and end words. Return 0 if no sequence exists, including when the end word is not in the list. The begin word does not need to be in the list.

examples.explanation: hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog has 5 words.

hints: Treat each word as a node, with an edge between words that differ by one letter.
Breadth-first search from the begin word finds the shortest sequence.
To find neighbours, try replacing each letter of the current word with each of the 26 letters and check whether the result is in the allowed set.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Given a non-empty list of positive integers, return True if it can be split into two groups whose sums are equal, otherwise False. Every number must go into exactly one group.

examples.explanation: The groups [1, 5, 5] and [11] both sum to 11.

hints: If the total is odd, the answer is False right away.
Otherwise the question becomes: can some subset add up to total / 2?
Keep a boolean table of reachable sums. For each number, update it from the largest sum down to the smallest so a number is not used twice.

title: Permutations of a List
description: Given a list of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) of its elements. Sort the resulting list of permutations in ascending order, comparing permutations like lists (so [1, 2, 3] comes before [1, 3, 2]). An empty list has exactly one permutation, the empty list.
hints: Choose the first element, then permute what remains.
Track which elements are still unused. When none are left, you have finished one permutation.
Remember to sort the final list of permutations.
